content: uv workspaces let a monorepo share one lockfile across many packages. The repository root declares [tool.uv.workspace] with members = ["services/*", "evals"], so every service and the eval harness resolve dependencies from the same uv.lock. Adding a member is a one-line change to the members list, but the lockfile must be regenerated afterwards with uv lock, because the resolve set changed. Day-to-day commands run from the repo root: uv sync --all-packages installs every workspace member into a single virtualenv, while uv run --project services/retriever scopes the run to one member. That scoping matters because each service keeps its own pyproject.toml with its own dependency list: ingestion needs confluent-kafka and langchain-text-splitters, the retriever needs sentence-transformers, and the generator needs langchain-openai. The workspace does not merge those lists; it only guarantees they resolve together without version conflicts. CI relies on the same property: one uv sync --all-packages step provisions the environment for every later pytest invocation, which is why dependency installation dominates the job runtime. The tradeoff of a shared virtualenv is that only one service root can be on sys.path per pytest run, so each suite keeps its own invocation rather than one combined sweep.

Reproducible CI starts with a lockfile that is always in sync. The lint job runs uv lock --check, which fails the build if any pyproject.toml changed without re-locking, so a dependency addition can never slip in unrecorded. Every install and every run then passes --frozen: uv sync --all-packages --frozen and uv run --frozen refuse to update the lockfile implicitly, meaning the exact resolved versions in uv.lock are the versions under test. That determinism is load-bearing for the eval harness, whose baselines are only comparable when the embedding library and tokenizer versions are identical across runs. The lockfile currently resolves just over a hundred packages; the dominant cost is the CPU PyTorch wheel pulled in by sentence-transformers, which is why CI installs dependencies once in the Python job and reuses that environment for unit tests, integration tests, and eval steps instead of repeating the install per job. A second lockfile would silently fork the resolve set, which is why a top-level evals directory had to join the workspace members rather than becoming its own project. When a dependency must change, the workflow is uv add --project <member> <package>, then commit both the pyproject.toml and the regenerated uv.lock together.

Ruff is the single Python linter, configured once at the repo root and applied everywhere with ruff check .. The selected rule sets are E for style errors, F for pyflakes correctness, and I for import sorting, with line-length 100 and target Python 3.12. Generated protobuf stubs under any gen/ directory are excluded via extend-exclude, because machine-generated code should never be linted. The most common violation in new code is I001, unsorted imports: ruff's isort implementation groups standard library, third-party, and first-party imports, and flat service modules like config or llm sort as first-party after third-party packages such as pytest. Running ruff check --fix resolves the mechanical cases automatically. CI runs the lint job before any tests because it needs none of the project dependencies and finishes in seconds, giving the fastest possible feedback on style regressions. Editor integration is straightforward, but the command line remains the source of truth: if uvx ruff check . passes locally, the CI job will pass too. Line-length violations (E501) usually mean an f-string or SQL statement should be wrapped, not that the limit should be raised.

gofmt -l exits 0 even when it lists files, so chaining it with && echo clean always prints clean. The gateway CI step works around this by capturing the output into a variable and failing explicitly when it is non-empty, then printing gofmt -d . so the log shows the required diff. That trap is worth naming because it is the exact shape of bug the eval discipline rule hunts: a check that cannot go red manufactures false confidence. The step also pins cache-dependency-path to gateway/go.sum so the Go module cache restores correctly across runs. Alongside formatting, the gateway job runs go build ./... and go vet ./... before go test ./...: the build catches compile breaks, vet catches suspicious constructs such as unreachable code or misused format strings, and the tests cover the query handler's gRPC-to-HTTP error mapping, which is easy to regress silently. Go 1.26.1 is pinned in the workflow via actions/setup-go. None of this needs Docker or Python, so the gateway job stays fast and independent of the Postgres service container that the Python job requires.

The integration marker separates tests that need live infrastructure from pure unit tests. Tests touching Postgres carry pytestmark = pytest.mark.integration, and CI runs the suite twice: once with -m "not integration" for the fast unit layer, and once with -m integration against a pgvector/pgvector:pg16 service container on port 5432. The marker itself is registered in the pytest ini options so an unregistered-mark typo fails loudly instead of silently selecting nothing. Integration coverage targets exactly the properties a unit test cannot assert: schema creation, the HNSW index definition, the 384-dimension vector column, idempotent upserts, and the foreign key from document_chunks to documents. The service container uses the same image, user, password, and database name as the local docker-compose file, so CI and a local run exercise the same database. A healthcheck on pg_isready with retries guards the classic race where the first test connects before Postgres finishes starting. Unit tests, by contrast, must never touch the network: they use fakes, stubs, and monkeypatched classes, which keeps them deterministic and fast enough to run on every save.

The three Python services share flat top-level module names — config, db, embedder, llm, main, server — so only one service root can be on sys.path per pytest run. A combined pytest services/ sweep would silently resolve import config to whichever service was collected first, producing passes that test the wrong module. The defense is structural: the root pyproject pins pythonpath per service, and every suite gets its own pytest invocation (pytest services/ingestion, pytest services/retriever, pytest services/generator, pytest evals). Each suite carries a conftest.py that inserts its own root at sys.path position zero; the generator and retriever conftests additionally evict other services/* roots, because the root ini's pythonpath entry is applied around conftest loading and would otherwise let ingestion's config shadow the local one. That shadowing went unnoticed while the generator tests only imported llm, a name unique to that service, and bit the moment a test imported the shared config name. Editable installs of all members exist in the workspace virtualenv, but a real directory at sys.path position zero wins over the editable finders, which is why the insert order is what matters.

The Python CI job provisions its database with a Postgres service container rather than installing Postgres on the runner. The image is pgvector/pgvector:pg16, chosen because the vector extension, the 384-dimension column type, and the HNSW index are enforced by the server — no unit test can assert them. Environment variables set POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and POSTGRES_DB to cortex, cortex_dev, and cortex, mirroring the local docker-compose file so CI and development exercise identical credentials. The service maps port 5432 to the runner, and the job exports DB_HOST localhost plus the same DB_PORT, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, and DB_PORT values explicitly rather than relying on conftest defaults, so a change to those defaults cannot silently repoint CI at the wrong database. Startup racing is handled with a container healthcheck: pg_isready -U cortex on a 10-second interval with 5 retries, without which the first test intermittently fails with connection refused while Postgres is still initializing. Because the database is a job-level service, every step in the job — unit tests, integration tests, eval seeding, and eval runs — shares it without paying container startup more than once.

CI runtimes are dominated by dependency installation, so both language jobs cache aggressively. The Python job enables the setup-uv cache, which persists the downloaded wheels across runs; the step that hurts most is sentence-transformers pulling a CPU PyTorch wheel, an install measured in minutes rather than seconds on a cold cache. That cost is paid exactly once per job because unit tests, integration tests, and the eval steps all reuse the single synced environment instead of each getting an isolated install. The Go job caches by a different key: actions/setup-go with cache-dependency-path pointed at gateway/go.sum, so the module cache invalidates precisely when the dependency set changes. Ruff needs none of this — the lint job runs uvx ruff check . with no project dependencies at all and finishes in seconds, which is why it is sequenced first for the fastest signal. The general rule the workflow follows is that cache keys must derive from lockfiles (uv.lock, go.sum), never from branch names or timestamps, so a cache hit always means an identical dependency set. Restoring a stale cache is worse than a cold install because it can mask a resolution change the lockfile was supposed to record.

Local infrastructure starts with docker compose -f infra/local/docker-compose.yml up -d, which brings up Postgres and Kafka as named containers on the default bridge network. Readiness is not the same as container-Is-running, so the run script waits explicitly: Postgres is polled with docker exec cortex-postgres pg_isready -U cortex, and Kafka with kafka-broker-api-versions against localhost:9092, because the broker answers API versions well before it finishes its own startup. Only after both answer does the script create the document.uploaded topic with --create --if-not-exists, one partition and replication factor one. Creating the topic up front matters: broker auto-creation only triggers on first produce or subscribe, so a consumer that subscribes first logs UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PART on its initial poll. The same ordering discipline continues into services — ingestion and retriever start before the gateway, and each listener is awaited on its port (50051 for the retriever after its embedding model loads, which can take three minutes cold). Ctrl-C stops the services while leaving Postgres and Kafka running; make down stops those too.

The run script builds the gateway to a file before starting it instead of using go run ., because go run compiles to a temporary binary and executes it as a child process. The PID the script tracks would then belong to the go tool rather than the server, and Ctrl-C cleanup would kill the wrapper while leaving the real gateway still holding port 8080. Building first with go build -o logs/gateway-bin . means the tracked PID is the server itself, so SIGTERM reaches the process that bound the port. The same pidfile discipline applies to the Python services: each start writes logs/<name>.pid, shutdown walks the list in reverse dependency order so the gateway stops before the services it calls, and any survivor gets SIGKILL after a grace period. Logs for every service land in logs/<service>.log from the first byte, because a cold retriever spends its startup downloading nothing but loading the embedding model — and a failure there must be visible without re-running anything. The script also exits as soon as any tracked PID dies, so a crashed process is never mistaken for a healthy stack waiting on a port that will never open.

Vector search runs on a pgvector HNSW index declared as USING hnsw with the vector_cosine_ops operator class. HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) trades a small recall loss for logarithmic query time, which is the right tradeoff for a top-k retrieval path that runs on every query. The retrieval SQL orders by the cosine distance operator embedding <=> %s::vector and converts to similarity for callers with 1 - distance, yielding scores in [0, 1] where 1 means identical. The LIMIT clause takes top_k directly as a bound parameter, and the query embedding itself is bound twice — once for scoring, once for ordering. The embedding column is fixed at vector(384) to match all-MiniLM-L6-v2 output, and both the ingestion and retriever services validate that dimension at model load so a misconfigured model name fails at startup instead of mid-query. The index is created IF NOT EXISTS alongside the tables, so repeated startups and CI runs converge on the same schema. Exact search would scan every row; the HNSW index is what keeps retrieval latency flat as the chunk count grows into the tens of thousands.

Postgres creates a B-tree index by default for primary keys and unique constraints, and B-trees remain the right structure for equality and range predicates on sortable columns. The documents table relies on this twice over: its TEXT primary key gets a B-tree automatically, and the UNIQUE constraint on (doc_id, chunk_index) in document_chunks gets one as well, which is what makes the chunk upsert's ON CONFLICT target enforceable. Unlike vector similarity, which needs the HNSW index and the cosine distance operator, ordinary lookups such as SELECT content FROM documents WHERE id = %s are served by plain B-tree descent with no extension required. The query planner consults pg_stats histograms to choose between an index scan and a sequential scan, and small tables are often scanned sequentially no matter what indexes exist — which is why integration tests assert index presence from pg_indexes rather than inferring it from query plans. A common mistake is adding indexes for the write path's benefit: every index slows ingestion, so the schema carries exactly three — the primary key, the upsert conflict target, and the HNSW vector index — and nothing speculative.

The ingestion worker consumes as part of a named consumer group, defaulting to ingestion-worker via KAFKA_GROUP_ID. Group membership is what gives the pipeline its delivery semantics: the broker tracks one committed offset per partition per group, so restarting the worker resumes where it left off instead of reprocessing the whole topic. That resume behavior is why re-ingestion is idempotent downstream — the database upserts tolerate replays, and stale high-index chunks are deleted, so an at-least-once redelivery converges on the same rows. During local startup the consumer's first poll can log UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PART, which is benign: it means the consumer subscribed before the topic existed, and the run script now pre-creates the topic to silence it. Consumer lag is the operational metric to watch — if the worker falls behind the produce rate, ingest returns 202 while documents wait unprocessed, and queries 404 against an index that has not caught up. The group id also isolates test traffic: integration and eval fixtures use distinct group ids so a test consumer never steals partitions from the development worker.

The document.uploaded topic is the sole seam between the gateway and the ingestion worker. The gateway's ingest handler validates that doc_id and content are present, serializes them to JSON, and produces to the topic configured by KAFKA_TOPIC, returning 202 accepted as soon as the broker acknowledges — long before chunking or embedding happens. Locally the topic is created with one partition and replication factor one, which is correct for development and wrong for production in exactly one way: a single partition caps throughput at one consumer's speed and offers no redundancy. The run script creates the topic explicitly with kafka-topics --create --if-not-exists rather than relying on broker auto-creation, because auto-creation only fires on first produce or subscribe and leaves a confusing UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PART error in the consumer log meanwhile. Retention is the broker default, so documents accumulate until the volume is reclaimed; nothing in the pipeline deletes from the topic after processing. The consumer group, not the topic, tracks progress — rewinding means resetting the group's offsets, not republishing documents.

The gateway's query handler runs retrieval and generation under one shared 30-second context deadline. Both gRPC calls receive the same context, so a slow retriever steals time from the generator and vice versa — the budget is global, not per hop. That sharing is why large reasoning models on rate-limited free tiers are dangerous here: a 60-second chain-of-thought routinely exhausts the budget and surfaces as a wall of 504s that look like outages but are really the deadline working as designed. The handler treats an empty retrieval result as a client-visible condition, not a failure: zero chunks returns 404 with a message telling the caller to ingest documents, and the generator is never called. A downed generator, by contrast, is a 503 — the distinction matters for alerting, because 404s mean an empty index while 503s mean a dead dependency. The 30-second value is a hardcoded constant, not configuration; changing the latency envelope means editing the handler, which keeps the tradeoff visible in code review rather than hidden in an environment variable.

Every gRPC failure from the retriever or generator is translated to an HTTP status at the gateway boundary by one mapping function, and that mapping is covered by stubbed-client tests because it regresses silently. InvalidArgument becomes 400, NotFound 404, AlreadyExists 409, ResourceExhausted 429, DeadlineExceeded 504, Unavailable 503, and anything unrecognized falls through to 502. The 429 arm exists for the future: OpenRouter free-tier rate limits surface as resource exhaustion, and the generator's retry-with-backoff exists to absorb them before they ever reach this mapping. Message sizes are bounded per service — 4 MB each way on the retriever, 8 MB on the generator — so an enormous context fails fast with a clear resource error instead of stalling the shared deadline. The GenerateAnswer request also carries an optional model override field, but the override stays within the server's configured provider: a model ID alone does not say which API serves it, so cross-provider overrides are rejected by construction rather than attempted. Structured output is a similar contract point: the chain parses into a fixed Pydantic schema, and any provider that cannot honor response_format cannot serve this endpoint.

All embeddings come from all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a 384-dimensional sentence transformer chosen because it is small, fast on CPU, and good enough for passage retrieval. The dimension is load-bearing across the whole system: the Postgres column is vector(384), both services validate the model's output dimension at startup and raise ValueError on mismatch, and the eval golden set pins the model name so a swap invalidates every label and baseline loudly instead of silently. Query and document paths must use the same model — the two embedder modules are separate implementations, and a mismatch would surface as a silent recall collapse rather than an error, which is why a parity test drives both through encode with byte-identical arguments. The encode call itself passes show_progress_bar=False and convert_to_numpy=True, returning plain float lists with no numpy dependency leaking to callers. First use downloads roughly 80 MB of weights from HuggingFace Hub into the local cache; every later load is local and fast, but a cold retriever startup still budgets minutes for model loading before it starts listening on port 50051.

Documents are split with RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter at 500 characters with 50 characters of overlap, measured with len. The overlap exists so a sentence straddling a boundary remains retrievable from either adjacent chunk; without it, queries matching boundary text systematically miss. Re-ingestion is handled by index arithmetic, not by wiping the document: chunks are upserted on the (doc_id, chunk_index) conflict target, and any stored rows with a higher index than the new batch are deleted first, so shortening a document cannot orphan stale chunks. Chunk identity is the unstable part of the design: the id column is a SERIAL surrogate that shifts on every reseed, which is why eval labels reference (doc_id, chunk_index) pairs and never chunk_id. Changing CHUNK_SIZE re-indexes every chunk in the corpus and invalidates all golden labels at once — the golden metadata pins the chunking parameters precisely so that invalidation is a loud refusal instead of a silent metric drift. Empty or whitespace-only documents produce zero chunks rather than an error, leaving the caller to decide what emptiness means.
